'''Jim Watson''', [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]], (20 April 1936—18 December 2020)<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=McKellar |first1=A. R. W. |last2=Oka |first2=Takeshi |year=2023 |title=James Kay Graham Watson. 20 April 1936—18 December 2020 |url=https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/10.1098/rsbm.2022.0038 |journal=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society |volume=74|pages=419–438 |doi=10.1098/rsbm.2022.0038 |doi-access=free }}</ref> who published under the name '''J.K.G. Watson''', was a molecular spectroscopist most well known for the development of the widely used [[molecular Hamiltonian]]s named after him (sometimes called "Watsonians" or "Watson Hamiltonians"). These Hamiltonians are used to describe the quantum dynamics of molecules.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Meyer |first=Henning |date=October 2002 |title=THE MOLECULAR HAMILTONIAN |url=https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/10.1146/annurev.physchem.53.082201.124330 |journal=Annual Review of Physical Chemistry |language=en |volume=53 |issue=1 |pages=141–172 |doi=10.1146/annurev.physchem.53.082201.124330 |pmid=11972005 |issn=0066-426X|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Education and career==
Watson did his PhD at the [[University of Glasgow]], and worked in the UK, United States and Canada. He was a [[postdoctoral fellow]] under [[Jon Hougen]] in the Molecular Spectroscopy Group of [[Gerhard Herzberg]] at the National Research Council of Canada in [[Ottawa]], Ontario from 1963 to 1965. He eventually joined the staff in the group in 1982 where he remained until retirement.

Watson published a number of papers in which he developed and applied molecular Hamiltonians to problems in spectroscopy. In 1968 Watson published ''Simplification of the molecular vibration-rotation Hamiltonian'', in which he presented a practical framework for the quantum-mechanical description of molecular ro-vibrational dynamics within the [[Born–Oppenheimer approximation]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Watson |first1=J.K.G. |title=Simplification of the molecular vibration-rotation hamiltonian |journal=Molecular Physics |year=1968 |volume=15 |issue=5 |pages=479–490 |doi=10.1080/00268976800101381 |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/00268976800101381 |access-date=5 September 2022|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Honors and awards==
He was a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]], the [[Royal Society of Canada]] and the [[American Physical Society]].<ref name=":0" /> He received the 1986 Earle K. Plyer Prize for Molecular Spectroscopy and Dynamics from the American Physical Society. The citation reads:

"For his numerous fundamental contributions to the theory of rovibronic interactions in molecules, especially the development of the universally used Watson Hamiltonian for vibration-rotation energy levels, the unified treatment of centrifugal distortion in molecules, the elucidation of forbidden rotational transitions in spherical tops, the application of advanced symmetry arguments to perturbations in external fields, and investigations of the Jahn-Teller effect in <chem>H_3</chem> and <chem>NH_4</chem>."<ref>{{cite web |title=1986 Earle K. Plyler Prize for Molecular Spectroscopy & Dynamics Recipient: James K.G. Watson |url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Watson&first_nm=James&year=1986 |website=APS Physics |access-date=5 September 2022}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Watson was married to Carolyn Kerr. He died in his home in [[New Edinburgh]] after a brief illness on 17 December 2020 at the age of 84.<ref name=":0">{{cite web |title=Obituary – James (Jim) WATSON |url=https://ottawacitizen.remembering.ca/obituary/james-jim-watson-1081309128 |work=Ottawa Citizen |date=26 December 2020}}</ref>
